newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU wrestles over beef aid and size of British cull.
newsitem.headline: EU wrestles over beef aid and size of British cull.

text.p: European Union farm ministers on Monday wrestled with proposals to help farmers and beef markets hit by new evidence humans can develop a form of mad cow disease.

The evidence, announced by British scientists last week, strengthened the view of other EU countries that Britain must respect the bloc's Florence summit agreement in June on fighting the disease before any easing of a global ban on British beef.
"The Florence agreement has to be met. The accelerated cull has to go ahead," Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates, whose country currently holds the rotating EU presidency, told reporters.
German, Belgian and Spanish farm ministers agreed.
During a break in the meeting, British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg hinted Britain may drop some of the objections it has raised to the culling of extra cattle.
"We certainly haven't ruled out a (selective) cull and a cull may take place," he said
Under the Florence accord, Britain should kill up to 147,000 extra cattle to try to stem the fatal cattle brain disease.
But Hogg added that Britain must first clear a backlog -- estimated at nearly 400,000 cattle -- to be culled under a scheme for animals over 30 months old agreed earlier.

He said the extra cull would also have to be justified scientifically -- it was unclear whether Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) can be passed from cow to calf -- and this may not be possible until at least early 1997.
But Hogg added other countries may still insist on a cull.
"At that point we will have to decide whether to proceed," he said.
Hogg, heading a team of five British ministers, said Britain would press for progress on exempting grass-fed, BSE-free herds from the global ban
"We have identified the beef assurance scheme and certified herds as being those animals for which one could expect first to get a relaxation of the ban," Hogg told reporters.
Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth stressed the importance for Scottish farmers, noting that one third of agricultural income came from Angus beef and other grass-fed herds.
Forsyth said only 3,500 extra Scottish cattle would have to be slaughtered instead of 6,000 previously estimated because cattle had already been killed under the 30 months scheme.
But Fischler cautioned against any early progress.
"I don't think we will achieve very much today because I think we need more time," he told reporters.
Officials said progress was stalled until after EU scientists rule in mid-November on British research casting doubt on whether an extra cull of cattle was needed.
German Farm Minister Jochen Borchert insisted the British ban must be kept in place. "There can only be a relaxation if there is no risk coming from British beef exports," he said.
Spanish Farm Minister Loyola de Palacio said Britain must take all public health precautions, including the selective cull, agreed in Florence.
Fischler emphasised the urgent need to agree a package of measures to reduce beef production in line with a drop in demand due to consumer fears that BSE could be passed on to humans.
But member states were deeply critical of plans to fund the 1.3 billion Ecus ($1.6 billion) package, which includes a scheme to slaughter new-born calves, by cutting aid to cereals farmers.
Fischler said cereal cuts were needed because 1.7 billion Ecus of unspent 1996 funds could not be transferred to 1997.
